results.title: This Free App Unlocks A Useful Tap Feature On Your MacBook's Palm Rest
results.content:
X/Jaskirat Singh

Available for download from the developer's website or from GitHub, MacTap supports two types of gestures. If you're holding the laptop on your lap, you may want to tap on the palm rest to perform a specific shortcut. If the laptop sits still on a desk, tapping on the desk may be even more convenient, as the knock would reverberate through the chassis. The GitHub documentation says that MacTap will work on MacBook Air (M2 and later) and MacBook Pro (M1 Pro, M1 Max, and later) models, as motion sensor data has to be available to apps. That way, the software can listen for and interpret motions like taps and knocks and pair them with actions. [...] Advertisement

Users interested in enabling Back Tap gestures on their MacBooks, but who may be worried about downloading software from developers (or from GitHub) have a few alternatives, including apps that can be installed from the Mac App Store. InputConfig is one such example. It was launched in early July 2026, with tap support having been added in mid-September.

Separately, premium MacTap-like apps exist, in case you want to avoid free software. Tapcut is priced at $6.99 after a free trial period. It supports double, triple, and quadruple taps. Finally, Shortap, seen in the video above, is priced at $5 for one MacBook, and supports single, double, and triple taps for each side of the palm rest. [...] MacBooks don't have a native equivalent to Back Tap, and that's understandable. Interacting with a laptop may be even easier than interacting with a smartphone, as you have access to the trackpad, a full keyboard, and powerful keyboard shortcuts to help you control apps and multitask with speed. Also, the Back Tap name would not make sense, as tapping the back of the lid or the bottom side of the case would be cumbersome. That's why apps like MacTap, released in early September 2026, use the palm rest for taps.
